cards.explanation: The answer is that Tyre has been saying it is perfect in beauty. God quotes Tyre's own words: "You have said, O Tyre, ‘I am perfect in beauty.’" (Ezekiel 27:3) Notice the line is Tyre talking about itself. I once spent years in a junk drawer, and nobody caught me bragging about my looks back there.

The answer is ship. Planking, a mast, and in the next verses oars, a deck and a sail all belong on a vessel. God is describing Tyre like a grand ship, with cypress from Senir and a cedar from Lebanon doing the heavy lifting. Picture the lumber yard that order took.

The answer is Egypt. The sail is made of "…embroidered fine linen from Egypt…" and it serves as the ship's banner (Ezekiel 27:7). So the sail isn't just catching wind, friends, it's showing off. A sail doing double duty, that's a hard-working piece of cloth.

The answer is men of Tyre. The verse says, "Your men of skill, O Tyre, were there as your captains." (Ezekiel 27:8) So the oars are pulled by men from Sidon and Arvad, while Tyre's own skilled men steer. Even a ship this grand had a crew from all over.

The answer is True. The elders of Gebal come aboard as shipwrights, "…repairing your leaks." (Ezekiel 27:9) So even a ship called perfect in beauty needs patching. Perfect in beauty, and still calling the repair crew.

The answer is to barter for its merchandise. "All the ships of the sea and their sailors came alongside to barter for your merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:9) They come to trade, not to fight. It's a busy harbor, and Tyre's goods are what bring the ships in. Picture a whole fleet lining up like customers at the bakery door on a holiday morning.

The answer is True. Of the warriors from Persia, Lydia and Put, the text says, "they gave you splendor." (Ezekiel 27:10) The men on the walls hang their shields around them, and the text says "they perfected your beauty." (Ezekiel 27:11) Even the armor is part of the decorating.

The answer is the east wind. "Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea." (Ezekiel 27:26) God names the east wind. The oarsmen got the ship way out there, and the wind is what shatters it. It's a sudden turn after a very big, busy picture.

The answer is True. Tyre's wealth, wares and merchandise, its sailors, captains and shipwrights, its merchants and all the warriors will "…sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall." (Ezekiel 27:27) The list is long, the same way the building of the ship was. I think that's a heavy verse, friends, and it's worth sitting with.

The answer is shore. "All who handle the oars will abandon their ships. The sailors and all the captains of the sea will stand on the shore." (Ezekiel 27:29) First they leave their ships, then they stand on the shore. The ones who ran the sea end up standing on land. That's a big change of scenery.

The answer is bitter mourning over Tyre. The text says, "They will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning." (Ezekiel 27:31) Dust on heads, ashes and sackcloth all go with that grief. I think this one is heavy.

The answer is enriched. The sailors say, "You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise." (Ezekiel 27:33) They also say, "…you satisfied many nations." The lament remembers what Tyre's trade gave to others.

The answer is that they are appalled. In the lament, "All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you." (Ezekiel 27:35) The kings shudder with fear and their faces are contorted. It's shock all around the coast.

The answer is False, and I'm sorry it's such a heavy one. The lament closes with, "you have come to a horrible end and will be no more." (Ezekiel 27:36) Those who trade among the nations hiss at Tyre, and no rising again is mentioned. That's where the sailors' lament stops.
